chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Electronic instruments versus acoustic ones
summary: Wilson and Hinton argue electronics offer novelty but acoustic instruments let a player stamp individuality, with Ray Brown's advice on amplifiers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now you're coming my way, because that's what I was thinking, that perhaps the young people coming out of college might be getting into big business, and they might have an idea about bringing back some of the creative stuff.
And that could change this around, like you were saying it may be on its way out, anyway.

The only thing is, they're also intrigued with this electronic thing now. To me, this electronic thing is kind of opposed to good music, because the solo comes out, but the wooden bass fiddle, the regular old fashioned piano, the strings or a trumpet with a mouthpiece, where you can manipulate the tone, your individual way, to stamp your individuality on the instrument - but the electric instruments, the electronics call for all different values in order for them to express individuality. It can be done -- if they can do that, otherwise the electric instrument becomes only a novelty, a new sound that wears thin, you know, after awhile, after you hear a new sound, it's no longer new, you got to get another new sound, get a new new sound.
But the old stuff wears better.

You don't have the power, the creativity, of creating your own power. You evolve with this that can blow the world up--- atomic age of progress, take an amplifier and turn it up, so one bass player can blow out 16 bands, see.
Sure. I remember Ray Brown used to say don't teach anybody who played bass with an amplifier on it, he's got to learn to play it so he can make his own
power first, before anything else, and what he does later with it is his own business.

But if he's gonna learn to learn a bas$ -- an acoustical bass, we got to teach him so that he can be able to get his own power, so when he is able to get his own dynamics, he knows it's going to take his strength to do that, not turn a dial or step on a pedal.
That's beautiful, Teddy, and it's so nice to hear you say these things, because I think that's what young people really want to know about you -- how you feel about this business.
